o: We must unpivot a table with an unknown, dynamic set of store columns (1 to 30, names vary per test) into rows of (product_id, store, price), dropping NULL cells. Because column names are unknown at write time, a static UNION ALL query cannot work — the SQL itself must be generated at runtime from metadata. Example 1 shows four store columns collapsing into six data rows, skipping nulls.
k: Static SQL cannot reference unknown column names; generate the query text dynamically.
INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS lists the actual column names of the Products table at runtime.
GROUP_CONCAT builds one big UNION ALL statement, prepared and executed dynamically.

a.n: Dynamic SQL via INFORMATION_SCHEMA + Prepared Statement
a.i: Query INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS for all columns of Products except product_id. For each, emit a SELECT that renames the column to 'store', selects its value as price, and filters IS NOT NULL. Concatenate these with UNION ALL using GROUP_CONCAT (raising group_concat_max_len so the statement is not truncated), then PREPARE/EXECUTE the generated text.
s: Raise group_concat_max_len to safely hold the generated SQL.
Select column names from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS where table_name='Products' and column_name<>'product_id'.
Build per-column SELECT fragments joined by UNION ALL into @sql.
PREPARE and EXECUTE @sql inside the procedure.

c.cpp: -- SQL problem: MySQL solution is in the python field.

a.t: One metadata scan plus one execution of a UNION ALL over all store columns — effectively O(rows × stores).

w: Pitfalls: forgetting to exclude product_id from the generated fragments, default group_concat_max_len (1024) truncating the query with many stores, and quoting literals ('store names need doubled single quotes inside CONCAT'). Follow-ups may ask for the reverse (PIVOT), which requires conditional aggregation with the same dynamic-generation trick.
